newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW says GM Canada doesn't need to outsource.
newsitem.headline: CAW says GM Canada doesn't need to outsource.

text.p: As negotiations between General Motors Corp's Canada unit and the Canadian Auto Workers union approach a midnight Wednesday strike deadline, the war of words is mounting over outsourcing, which remains the biggest stumbling block to a deal.

With less than three days left to ink a deal, the CAW issued a report to reporters on Monday that contradicted GM Canada's assertion that it needed to outsource jobs on the components side of its production and sell several parts plants to remain competitive.

"That's not a valid argument in Canada," CAW president Buzz Hargrove told reporters during a break in bargaining. "If you look at the Canadian operations, they are currently lower today in in-house production of components than where they are trying to get to in the U.S."

The CAW report showed only 47 percent of GM's Canadian workforce was engaged in parts production, compared to 68 percent in the United States. The union said that since Canada's parts work was already below GM's benchmark U.S. goals, the company's desire to lower its proportion of parts work in North America should not affect jobs in Canada.

"Even if GM's U.S. parent achieves its desired outsourcing goal -- shedding as many as 40,000 parts jobs in the U.S. -- the relative importance of parts-related employment will still be much greater in the U.S. than in Canada," the union said in the report.

But GM Canada's chief negotiator at the talks, Dean Munger, said the outsourcing issue was not about cutting the amount of work done inside GM's plants, known as vertical integration. "We're not talking about the vertical integration percentages and I heard Buzz refer to those. We're dealing with the competitiveness issue," said Munger.
GM Canada's 1995 profit of C$1.39 billion was the highest ever recorded by a Canadian company.

"We need to sustain that profit and we have to build upon it so that we can be in a good position... when we get into these economic downturns," said Munger. "The plans that we have set in place are dealing with that so that we can provide a competitive product at a competitive price."
GM Canada has said it intends to sell two parts plants in Canada and outsource work at a cost of about 5,500 jobs.
Hargrove said those decisions must be reversed or altered before a new collective agreement is signed.

"GM has two options: they can reverse the decisions, or they can sell the plants and allow the workers to remain workers under (the GM-CAW master agreement) for the life of the agreement," said Hargrove.
Munger said GM intends to sell the plants as ongoing businesses and shed those jobs.
"To have an arrangement that they would be our employees on an ongoing basis is inconsistent with the objectives that we want to accomplish," he said.
Analysts have speculated that GM cannot afford a deal based on one reached two weeks ago by the CAW and Chrysler.

The Chrysler agreement gave the union unprecedented say into outsourcing decisions by the company and is considered the framework for the current talks between the CAW and GM. Chrysler and Ford contracted out much of their work over the past 20 years during tough times in order to cut costs, and as a result both now outsource more work than does GM.

But the union said GM's assertions that it now has to downsize in order to compete ignore the fact that GM's hourly workforce in Canada has declined by about 12,500 over the past decade, a decline approximately equal to the entire current workforce of either Ford or Chrysler.
